note: Comparison inputs (Project & Scientific Guide §06). Weights are a project methodology decision with a written rationale per task (owner may adjust). Each assessment picks one named rubric level (strong=1, close=0.75, partial=0.5, weak=0.25, mismatch=0) and cites a source on BOTH the Earth side and the planetary side. Any dimension with no assessment is UNKNOWN, never zero; a candidate below 50% weighted coverage is reported as insufficient evidence and not ranked.

weights.rationale: Guide §06: surface processes (dune migration, erosion/deposition) drive aeolian research; dune geometry next; wind/atmosphere context interprets the process; materials matter least.
Guide §06: channel morphology, sedimentology and geological context matter more than mobility; environment only frames interpretation.
Guide §15: documented subsurface structure first, then materials (attenuation), dry conditions, then crater morphology.
Guide §04: slope, roughness and obstacles first, then loose material/bearing strength, then operating environment; surface processes least.
Guide §05 (soil, drilling, sampling): physical material properties first, then layering and environment (aridity, biomass context).
Environment-defined task: temperature/aridity context first; materials and processes interpret it.
Drilling into ice-cemented ground depends on subsurface layering, material properties and cold environment.
Volcanic analog work compares lava materials first, then flow morphology and emplacement processes.

assessments.rationale: Wind-formed barchan dunes are documented on both sides (Western Desert barchan chains; Bagnold barchan and linear dunes). Same bedform type, but Mars wind transport acts in a much thinner atmosphere.
Crescent (barchan) dune form appears on both sides, but dune height, spacing and slopes are not quantified in the sources reached.
El-Baz et al. directly compare Egyptian barchan dunes with dunes in Viking images of the north polar sand sea: same wind-formed bedform type.
Barchan forms on both sides; dune dimensions and relief are not quantified in the abstract.
Both preserve deposits of ancient flowing water, but an inverted channel and a lake delta are different landforms (Project Scope §12).
Inverted channel ridges vs. a 45 km crater containing a delta: shapes and scales differ.
Both preserve ancient fluvial deposits (Egyptian inverted stream channels; Arabia Terra fluvial depositional systems). Kept at 'partial' because the Arabia Terra source was read only in part.

GPR has imaged shallow layered structure on both sides to roughly 15 m (270 MHz GPR, 2-15 m at Gilf Kebir; RIMFAX to 15 m with layers inclined up to 15 degrees at Jezero). Materials, instruments and the origin of the Earth structures differ.
Small buried crater-like structures vs. a 47.5 km impact crater: crater morphology at very different scales.
Small crater-like structures vs. a 155 km impact crater. S02 compares Gilf Kebir to heavily eroded mid-latitude cratered terrains, not to Gale.
Voigt et al. compare Holuhraun lava morphologies (transitional/rubbly flows, polygonal terrain) directly with young volcanic terrains in Elysium Planitia.
Fissure-fed eruption and lava-water interaction are discussed for both settings in the same study.
